t.bedik bandafassi@12.6,-12.4:
In the hills of south-eastern Senegal, near the border with Guinea, the Bedik people live in villages perched on rocky hilltops, reached by steep paths through the bush. Their round huts with tall conical thatched roofs, clustered closely together, and their traditions of masks, initiation and seasonal festivals have survived because of their isolation. The Bedik country around Bandafassi is part of the Bassari Country: Bassari, Fula and Bedik Cultural Landscapes, listed by UNESCO in 2012, along with the lands of their Bassari and Fula neighbours.

The landscape is a mix of savannah, wooded hills and river valleys, at the edge of the Fouta Djallon highlands that rise across the border in Guinea. It is greener than most of Senegal, especially in the rainy season, and wildlife is still found in the area, particularly in the nearby Niokolo-Koba National Park, one of the largest protected areas in West Africa. Nearby, near the village of Dindéfello, a waterfall plunges from a cliff into a cool pool, a popular spot for a swim after a hot ride.

Visiting the Bedik villages is a matter of respect. Go with a local guide, who can introduce you to the village chief and explain customs, and ask before taking photographs. In the villages of Iwol and others, the visit may involve a fee that supports the community. Festivals, often held around the beginning and end of the rainy season, are spectacular, but are primarily for the community, not tourists.

The riding here is rough and rewarding. Kédougou, the regional capital, is reached by a long paved road from Tambacounda, and from there, roads to the villages and the waterfall are a mix of tarmac, laterite and dirt tracks, dusty in the dry season and muddy, slippery and sometimes impassable in the rainy season from about July to October. Heat is intense, especially from March to June, and riding should be done in the early morning or late afternoon. A dual-sport bike is ideal.

Kédougou, about twenty-seven kilometres away, is the only real base, with fuel, shops, markets and guesthouses. Carry plenty of water and some food, and fill the tank before setting out. Gold mining has transformed the region in recent years, bringing traffic, trucks and change. In the evening, in Kédougou, try a plate of yassa, chicken or fish marinated in lemon and onions, or mafé, a rich peanut stew, the classic dishes of Senegal.
t.niokolo koba national park@13.0,-13.0:
In the south-east of Senegal, where the country presses against Guinea, the Gambia river begins to gather itself, and around its upper reaches lies Niokolo-Koba, one of the largest and oldest national parks in West Africa. It covers nearly a million hectares of savanna, dry forest, gallery woodland and grassy floodplain, and it holds some of the last strongholds of West African wildlife. UNESCO recognised it in 1981, and it has been listed as in danger since 2007, mostly because of poaching and pressure from outside.

The animals are the reason to come. Lions, leopards, hippos and elephants still live here, though in small numbers, and the park is home to the Derby eland, the largest antelope in the world, which survives in few places. Chimpanzees live in the forest corridors, and the birdlife is rich, with hornbills, kingfishers, bee-eaters and many other species. Sightings are not guaranteed, and the vegetation can be dense, but the rewards, when they come, are exceptional. The best time to look is the late dry season, from February to April, when animals gather at the remaining water.

The road is its own adventure. The main national road from Tambacounda to Kedougou crosses the park, and in places it is rough, patched and potholed, with long distances between settlements. Tracks within the park are usually dirt or sand, and many are impassable in the rainy season, from June to October, when the park is largely closed. Heat is intense in the dry months, and the harmattan wind brings dust and haze. A guide is normally required for park entry, and the rules are strictly enforced.

There are no real services within the park, and fuel is limited to the towns, mainly Tambacounda and Kedougou, so carry spare fuel, plenty of water and basic spares. Out toward Dindefello, near the Guinean border, there is a waterfall and a small chimpanzee reserve, and the hills there are green and cooler. Check the security and access situation, particularly near the borders, before you go, and plan with local help.
t.my son sanctuary@15.8,108.1:
My Son is a valley ringed by green hills in Quang Nam province, and the first thing that strikes you is the quiet. After the traffic of Da Nang and the tourist streets of Hoi An, a muddy path leads into a hollow where red-brick towers lean out of the trees. The temples were built by the Cham, a seafaring Hindu kingdom that ruled much of central Vietnam for over a thousand years, and who used this valley as a place for royal ceremonies and worship of Shiva.

Building went on from about the fourth century to the thirteenth, so the complex shows many styles. The bricks are fine and tightly fitted, and archaeologists still argue about how the Cham bonded them, since the walls show almost no mortar. Many of the towers were destroyed in 1969, when American bombing hit the area during the war, and craters are still visible beside the surviving buildings. Walking through it feels a bit like stepping around a half-finished conversation. Carved sandstone figures of dancers and gods, some worn nearly smooth, have been gathered in a small museum on site.

The ride from Hoi An takes the best part of an hour on busy roads, past rice paddies, water buffalo, cafes and roadside stalls. Surfaces are generally fine, though lorries and scooters mean you must keep your wits about you. Arrive early, ideally at opening, to beat the heat and the tour buses that fill the site by mid-morning. The dry season, roughly February to August, is easier; autumn brings typhoons and flooded roads.

Hoi An, twenty-seven kilometres away, has fuel stations, restaurants and plenty of beds. Along the way, small towns like Duy Xuyen have petrol and noodle shops. Try cao lau, the thick local noodle dish, before heading back, and bring water and a hat for the walk because shade is patchy.
t.dingle@52.1,-10.3:
Dingle is a small harbour town at the western end of County Kerry's Dingle Peninsula, with fewer than two thousand people but about as many pubs as you could want. The streets slope toward the water, shops and houses are painted in strong colours, and the harbour is full of fishing boats. This is a Gaeltacht area, where Irish is still the everyday language for many families, so you may see signs in Irish first, and the town's Irish name, An Daingean, appears on the road markers.

The peninsula is one of Ireland's richest landscapes for history. There are thousands of ancient monuments, from standing stones and ring forts to early Christian beehive huts, and the Gallarus Oratory, a stone chapel shaped like an upturned boat, has stood for over a thousand years without mortar. Out to sea, the Blasket Islands lie in the Atlantic, abandoned in 1953 but loved for the writers who grew up there. For decades, a bottlenose dolphin called Fungie lived in the harbour and was the town's most famous resident, and boat trips still go out to look for wildlife.

The ride around Slea Head is a classic, narrow and exposed with the ocean on one side and the mountain on the other. Beyond it the road climbs over the Conor Pass, at about 410 metres the highest pass in Ireland, with a narrow, twisting road and a drop to a glacial lake. It is a spectacular road but one-lane in places, so go carefully, and avoid it in thick fog or high winds. Summer brings tour buses, so start early. Weather is changeable, with soft rain and fast-moving sun, so a waterproof is essential.

Dingle has fuel, a few supermarkets, and countless cafes and bed-and-breakfasts. In high season rooms fill quickly. Cahersiveen, twenty-odd kilometres to the southwest across the water, also has fuel. Try a plate of fresh seafood at one of the harbour restaurants, a local ice cream, and a pint in a pub where there may be a session of traditional music in the evening.
t.da nang@16.1,108.2:
Da Nang is a port city on Vietnam's central coast, with a long beach, a wide river and a skyline that has changed dramatically in a generation. Where fishing boats and a French colonial quarter once stood, towers and bridges now line the Han River, and the Dragon Bridge, opened in 2013, spans the water in the shape of a golden dragon that breathes fire and water on weekend evenings. Behind the city, the green mass of the Son Tra peninsula rises above the sea.

The city has a long past as a trading port, and it was the site of a major American air base during the war. Older still is the Cham heritage, and the Museum of Cham Sculpture holds the world's largest collection of Cham art, with carved sandstone figures of gods, dancers and animals from the temples scattered across central Vietnam. South of the city the Marble Mountains, five limestone and marble hills, hold caves with Buddhist shrines and a stone-carving village at their feet.

From here the ride to My Son takes you inland through the Quang Nam countryside, past Hoi An's outskirts and into the farmland of the Thu Bon river valley, where rice, water buffalo and roadside stalls fill the view. North of the city lies the Hai Van Pass, a famous coastal road over a spur of mountains, with sea views and old French fortifications at the top, though most traffic now uses the tunnel beneath. Roads in the region are busy, so watch for scooters, trucks and sudden stops. Surfaces are generally good. The dry season, from about February to August, is best; typhoons can strike between September and November.

Da Nang has fuel everywhere, repair shops, hotels at all prices and good food. Try mi quang, a turmeric noodle dish topped with peanuts and herbs, or banh xeo, crisp pancakes wrapped in leaves. Traffic in the city is chaotic but moves at a manageable pace, and parking for bikes is easy. Start early to avoid the heat and the midday rush, and plan your return before dark.
t.wassu@13.7,-14.9:
Wassu stands beside the Gambia River in a country that is a narrow strip of land on either bank of the water, and the stone circles that give it fame belong to a landscape that most people never think about. The circles are rings of laterite pillars, some standing taller than a person, set in a grassy clearing and placed with a precision that suggests careful planning. Archaeologists believe they were burial monuments, raised over about a thousand years from the first millennium BC or soon after, by a society that has left no written records. In 2006, UNESCO listed the circles of Wassu, with those of Kerbatch, Sine Ngayène and Wanar in Senegal, as the Senegambian Stone Circles.

Each pillar was cut from laterite, the red crusted soil that covers much of West Africa, and carved or dressed to a roughly cylindrical shape. A few circles have a larger stone standing in the middle or a slab set at an angle, and some have been dug to show burials. At Wassu, a small museum on the site shows the finds. The stones are still red and rough, and in the low light of morning and evening they glow a deep brick colour against the green of the bush.

The ride along the river is slow, hot and flat, past villages of mud brick and tin roofs, fields of groundnuts and millet, baobabs and mango trees. The roads are mostly paved but have patches of broken surface, goats and donkeys, and shared taxis that stop without warning. The heat is intense, with temperatures above forty degrees before the rains, and the harmattan wind brings fine dust between November and February. Rains from June to October turn some tracks to mud. The river is crossed in places by ferry, so allow time and have cash for the fare.

Wassu is a small town, and fuel can be limited, so fill the tank at a larger town before heading up the river, and carry water. Simple meals of rice with fish or chicken, onion sauce and peanut stew are easy to find in the villages.

Aim for the cooler dry months from November to February, and visit early, before the sun is high.
t.tran hai fortress@16.6,107.7:
Trấn Hải Thành sits at the sea mouth of the Perfume River's lagoon system, a low old fort looking out over the beach at Thuận An, about twelve kilometres from the centre of Huế. It was built in the early nineteenth century under Emperor Gia Long, the founder of the Nguyễn dynasty, and rebuilt and strengthened under his son Minh Mạng, to guard the one waterway by which a hostile fleet could reach the imperial capital. In the middle of the century French ships showed what that fear was worth, and the Nguyễn defences fell in 1883 when the French attacked the estuary forts.

What you find today is quieter than the history. A square-ish brick and stone enclosure, partly restored, rises from sandy ground with casuarina trees nearby, and from the walls you can see the lagoon on one side and the open South China Sea on the other. Fishing boats pull up on the beach, and in the afternoon locals come out to sit under the shade and eat. It is not a polished attraction, and that is the charm.

The ride out from Huế is a pleasure by Vietnamese standards. Follow the river and then the long causeway-like road across the paddy and lagoon landscape, past tomb-like family graves, fish farms and rows of stilted houses. The surface is mostly good, but you share it with scooters, buses and the occasional water buffalo, so keep your speed honest and your eyes up. The Tam Giang lagoon, the largest in Southeast Asia, lies to the north and gives the whole area a wide, hazy light, especially at dawn.

Timing matters. Typhoons and heavy rain hit the coast most seriously between roughly September and November, and the beach road can be washed with sand after a storm. Between February and May, mornings are mild and the sky tends to be clear. Huế has plenty of fuel and food, including bún bò Huế, the spicy beef noodle soup that the city insists is the real thing. After the fort, return along the same road toward the citadel and the tombs of the Nguyễn emperors that fill the hills south of town.
t.hoi an ancient town@15.9,108.3:
Hội An is the one old port in Vietnam that was neither flattened by war nor remodelled in concrete, and that is why people tolerate the crowds. The town lies on the Thu Bồn river a short way from the sea, about twenty-five kilometres south of Da Nang. From the fifteenth to the nineteenth centuries it was a trading hub where Chinese, Japanese and later European merchants waited for the monsoon winds to turn. They left their marks in the architecture: yellow-walled Chinese assembly halls, narrow merchant houses with wooden beams, and the Japanese Covered Bridge, a small humped span that has become the town's emblem. The silt in the river eventually killed the harbour, and Da Nang took over the shipping. The decline saved the old streets, and UNESCO listed the town in 1999.

The best way to see it is by walking, because the heart of the old quarter is closed to motorbikes for part of the day and can be one-way or restricted in the evening. Park on the edge, lock the helmet, and go in at first light, when shopkeepers are sweeping and the markets are loud with herbs and fish. Cao lầu noodles are the local speciality, with the supposed secret being the water from a particular well, and the little white rose dumplings and the banh mi stalls are worth finding. After dark the lanterns come on and the river fills with paper boats and light.

Getting here from Da Nang is one of the pleasant rides in central Vietnam. The coast road runs south past the Marble Mountains and long beaches at China Beach, with sea air on one side and a tangle of small shops and resorts on the other. Expect heavy traffic, very patient scooters and the occasional sudden turn from a driver who has not looked. Hội An itself has fuel and every kind of food, and the ruined Cham temples at Mỹ Sơn are about forty kilometres inland on a ride that is best done early before the heat.

The wet season runs roughly from September to December, and floods sometimes put the riverside streets under water. February to April is easier.
t.tuktoyaktuk@69.4,-133.0:
The road ends at the Arctic Ocean, and that is why people come. Tuktoyaktuk, which everyone calls Tuk, is a small Inuvialuit community on the shore of the Beaufort Sea, at the top of the Mackenzie Delta, and for most of the twentieth century you could only reach it by boat, plane or a winter ice road across the frozen channels. In November 2017 the Inuvik-Tuktoyaktuk Highway opened, a gravel all-weather road of about 140 kilometres, and the Dempster Highway, which starts near Dawson City in the Yukon, finally had an end on salt water. Riders who have done the whole thing talk about it the way people talk about a pilgrimage.

The country is flat and enormous. North of Inuvik the spruce thins out and gives way to tundra, with willow scrub, small lakes and a horizon that seems to be a day's walk away. Beneath it is permafrost, ground that stays frozen all year, and it shapes everything: the road is built on a thick gravel pad to keep the heat of the sun from melting the ice below, buildings stand on piles, and the land heaves into odd shapes. The most curious of these are pingos, conical hills pushed up by ice under the surface. Near Tuk there is a cluster of them, including Ibyuk, which at roughly fifty metres is among the tallest in the world and is protected as a landmark.

Riding the last stretch means gravel, and gravel in the Arctic has its own character. The surface can be smooth and fast after grading, then loose, washboarded and wet within a few kilometres, and trucks throw stones. Tyre damage is a fact of life on the Dempster, so carry a repair kit and a spare tube. In summer the sun does not set for weeks, which makes timing strange, and the light at midnight is soft and low. Mosquitoes and black flies are fierce near still water, so keep your jacket zipped and your visor down when you stop.

Plan your fuel carefully. Inuvik is the last proper stop with real services, and it makes sense to fill the tank and any spare container there, rather than counting on anything at the end. The traditional ritual is to walk down to the shore and dip a hand or a boot in the Arctic Ocean, even in July, when the water is only a few degrees above freezing. Late June to August is the usual window, with long days and the road at its driest, and weather can turn quickly, with wind and cold rain coming off the sea. Respect the community, ask before photographing people, and leave nothing behind.
t.khe sanh@16.6,106.7:
Khe Sanh is a name that carries weight: for eleven weeks in the spring of 1968, a US Marine combat base on this plateau was besieged by North Vietnamese forces in one of the most closely watched battles of the war, and the red-earth hills around the town still bear the scars. A small museum on the site of the old base displays aircraft, bunkers and artefacts, and the overgrown airstrip is still visible. The place is quiet now, a market town of the Hướng Hóa district in Quảng Trị province, and the war is remembered with solemnity rather than spectacle.

Today the plateau is better known for coffee. The red basaltic soil and cool highland climate suit Arabica, and the hills around Khe Sanh are planted with coffee, pepper and cassava, with local cooperatives roasting and selling the beans. The town sits on Highway 9, the old road to Laos, which climbs from the coast through Đông Hà and reaches the border at Lao Bảo about thirty kilometres to the west. The Ho Chi Minh Road, a modern highway built on the line of the wartime supply trail, runs north and south through the mountains nearby.

For a rider on the route from Phong Nha toward A Lưới, Khe Sanh is a natural pause. The roads here are long and winding, through hills clothed in forest, with sudden valleys and waterfalls, and the surface is generally good on the main route, though patchy in places. Heavy rain, especially from September to December, can bring landslides, and mist often hangs on the heights. Dry-season months, from about February to May, are easier, though hot at lower altitudes.

Fuel is available in town, and it is wise to fill the tank, since stretches between stations can be long. Eat at a local café, with strong Vietnamese coffee and a bowl of noodles or rice and grilled pork, and the people are friendly. Respect the sites and the unexploded ordnance warnings: never stray off marked paths, as bombs and mines from the war still lie in the soil. Nearby, the old Lang Vei and Rockpile sites tell more of the story.
t.a luoi@16.3,107.2:
A Lưới lies in a long, narrow valley in the mountains of Thừa Thiên Huế province, close to the border with Laos, in country of steep forested ridges that catch the clouds. The valley is known by an older name, the A Shau, and it is remembered for the heavy fighting that took place here during the Vietnam War, when it served as a major corridor for the Ho Chi Minh trail. In May 1969, a battle for a hill nearby, known to American troops as Hamburger Hill, became a symbol of the war's costs. Today, A Lưới is a quiet district town with a market, fields of rice and a few memorial sites.

The valley is home to ethnic minorities, including the Pa Cô, Cơ Tu and Tà Ôi peoples, whose long houses and weaving traditions still survive. The Tà Ôi make a brightly patterned brocade called zèng, woven on backstrap looms, and visitors can sometimes see it made. The surrounding forest is rich in wildlife, though much of it was damaged by wartime defoliation, and regrowth is slow. Fog sits in the valley most mornings, lifting slowly, and the air smells of woodsmoke and wet earth.

For riders following the Ho Chi Minh Road, this is the end of a long and satisfying day. The road in is a wonderful ride, climbing and falling through jungle and across rivers, with long views over folded ridges. Surface quality varies: some stretches are smooth and new, others broken by landslides and washouts. Rain is frequent, especially in autumn and winter, and fog can reduce visibility sharply. Dry months are better, and a rain jacket is worth carrying all year. Huế, the old imperial capital, lies about seventy kilometres east.

Fuel is available in town, and a few small guesthouses and cafés provide rooms and meals. Plan to arrive before dark, as the mountain roads have livestock and unmarked hazards. Pay your respects at the local memorials, and stay on marked paths, since unexploded ordnance remains in the region. The best months for riding are February to May, when the skies are clearer, and the people are warm and welcoming to visitors who arrive with curiosity and care.
t.mahaxay@17.4,105.2:
Mahaxay is a small town in Khammouane province, in central Laos, about forty kilometres east of Thakhek, and it lies on the edge of one of the great limestone landscapes of South-East Asia. Vertical grey cliffs, covered with green vegetation, rise from flat rice fields and rivers, forming a jagged wall of karst towers. The scenery has a dreamlike quality, particularly in the early morning when mist hangs between the peaks and water buffalo wade in the paddies.

The Thakhek Loop is a popular motorbike route that circles through these hills, and Mahaxay is one of its natural stops, with a few guesthouses, noodle shops and a small market. The nearby area contains caves, including Tham Xang, the elephant cave, and the huge limestone caverns of the Hin Boun River, where boats are able to travel underground. Farther north is the Kong Lor cave, a river cave several kilometres long that you can pass through by boat, and one of the most remarkable sights in Laos.

The history here is sobering. During the Vietnam War, Laos was heavily bombed by the United States, and Khammouane province, which lay on the Ho Chi Minh Trail, was one of the worst affected areas. Unexploded bombs remain in the fields, and local people continue to live with the danger. Stay on established tracks and never touch metal objects. Many villages have been rebuilt, and the people are friendly and welcoming.

The road from Thakhek, Route 12, is mostly paved, with some rough patches and plenty of trucks heading to the Vietnam border, so ride carefully. The best season is from November to February, when the weather is cool and dry, while the monsoon from May to October brings heavy rain, flooding and mud. March and April are very hot and hazy.

Fill your tank in Thakhek before heading out, as fuel stops in smaller towns can be limited, and carry cash in kip. Sticky rice, grilled fish and fresh herbs are the local staples, and a cold Beerlao is the traditional end to the day.
t.nakai plateau@17.7,105.2:
The Nakai Plateau is a high, rolling upland in central Laos, at about 500 metres, in the south of Khammouane province, close to the Vietnamese border, and it is dominated by a huge reservoir. The Nam Theun 2 dam, completed in 2010, flooded a large part of the plateau, creating a lake with drowned forests and islands, and sold most of its electricity to Thailand. The villages that once stood here were resettled on higher ground, and the landscape has changed greatly.

Around the lake lies the Nakai-Nam Theun National Protected Area, a vast stretch of the Annamite mountains with some of the richest wildlife in South-East Asia. The forests shelter gibbons, tigers in very small numbers, and a number of rare species found nowhere else, including the saola, a shy forest ox that was found by scientists only in 1992 and is so elusive that few have seen it alive. The park is difficult to visit, and access is controlled, but the views of the mountains from the road are impressive.

The ride here is the far side of the Thakhek Loop. Beyond Mahaxay, the road climbs through karst hills, passing waterfalls and villages of stilted wooden houses, and rises to the plateau, where the air is cooler and the views are wide. The surface is mostly paved, with some potholes and gravel stretches, and trucks heading to Vietnam are frequent, so be cautious on bends. Rain can turn the red earth shoulders to mud, and mist often covers the hills in the morning.

Nakai town has a few shops, restaurants and basic guesthouses, and it is the main place to find fuel in this part of the loop, though supplies are not guaranteed and you should arrive with plenty. Cash in kip is useful, and mobile signal is patchy. Food is simple, with noodle soup, grilled meat and sticky rice.

The reservoir is calm and still at dawn, with mist lifting off the water and fishing boats gliding between drowned tree stumps. It is a quiet and rather haunting end to the route.
t.cahersiveen@51.9,-10.2:
Cahersiveen is the one town on the Iveragh peninsula that feels like a place rather than a stop, a long, low main street of coloured shopfronts and pubs, tucked under the rounded bulk of Bentee and Knocknadobar mountains, and looking out over the Fertha river and Valentia Harbour toward the island. About twelve hundred people live here, and a lot of them seem to be in the street on a fine afternoon. The Ring of Kerry has plenty of showier sights, but Cahersiveen has the habit of making visitors stay longer than they planned.

History sits all round the town. Daniel O'Connell, the great nineteenth-century campaigner for Catholic emancipation, was born at Carhan, a few kilometres east, and the town has a memorial church dedicated to him. The old police barracks, a fortress-like Victorian building with turrets, now houses a heritage centre that tells the story of the area and of the failed Fenian rising of 1867. Just outside the town are Ballycarbery Castle, a ruin standing in a field beside the estuary, and two ancient stone forts, Cahergall and Leacanabuaile, whose circular drystone walls are more than a thousand years old and wonderfully intact.

The riding on this side of the ring is the best of it. Beyond the town, the road swings out to Portmagee and the bridge to Valentia Island, then along cliffs with views of the Skellig rocks, which stand out in the Atlantic like jagged teeth. The Ring is usually ridden against the tour coaches, which are asked to run anticlockwise, so many riders go clockwise to avoid being stuck behind them. Mist and rain can sweep in from the ocean at any time of year, and the surface can be rough on the minor roads, so ride with care.

Cahersiveen has fuel stations and shops, so it is the sensible place to fill up before heading out to the headlands, and several cafés and pubs serve soup, brown bread and seafood. Dingle, across the bay, is a good deal further by road than it looks on the map, and the stretch between has little in the way of services. Late spring and early autumn are the best times, when the light is clear and the coaches are thinner on the ground.
t.waterville@51.8,-10.2:
Charlie Chaplin used to holiday in Waterville, and the town has not forgotten. A bronze statue of the comedian, in his bowler hat and cane, stands on the seafront, looking out across Ballinskelligs Bay, and each August the town holds a comedy festival in his honour. Chaplin came here with his family in the 1960s and enjoyed the fishing and the quiet. It is a small, neat seaside village strung along a narrow strip of land between the bay and a large freshwater lake, Lough Currane, and the combination of water, sand and mountains makes it one of the prettiest on the Iveragh Peninsula.

The lake is famous for its salmon and sea trout, and anglers come from across Europe to fish it. A short distance away, in the water, lie small islands, one with the ruins of an early Christian monastery. The village also has a links golf course, one of the best in Ireland, and a long promenade with views over the bay. Out to sea, the rocky Skellig islands stand like dark fangs on the horizon, and Skellig Michael, with its sixth-century monastery, is reached by boat from nearby ports in season.

On the Ring of Kerry, the stretch from Cahersiveen to Waterville is a highlight. The N70 follows the coast with wide views, passing the viewpoint at Coomakista Pass, a few kilometres further on toward Caherdaniel, where the whole sweep of the Atlantic, the Skellig islands and the cliffs of the peninsula spread out below. The road is wide, with a good surface, and bends that are broad and fast, though coaches and campervans in summer mean that overtaking is sometimes necessary. Early morning and late afternoon give the best light. The weather is Atlantic, so wind and rain are always a possibility.

The Iveragh coast is wild and beautiful, with sandy beaches, rocky headlands, gorse and fuchsia hedges, and views of the open ocean. Seabirds, including gannets and puffins, can be seen off the coast, and in summer, the sunsets over the bay are long and golden.

Waterville has fuel, small shops, pubs and cafés, serving seafood chowder, fresh crab and smoked salmon, and it is a sensible refuelling stop on the western stretch of the Ring. Cahersiveen, about seventeen kilometres to the north, is the next larger place. A walk along the seafront, past the statue, and a pint in a local pub completes the day.
t.ventry@52.1,-10.4:
Ventry is where the Slea Head loop really begins, a long curve of beach at the bottom of the Dingle Peninsula with the mountain Mount Eagle standing over its western end. The Irish name, Ceann Trá, means the head of the strand, and the beach is exactly that: a clean, wide sweep of sand, popular with families and swimmers in summer and often completely empty in the shoulder months. Dingle is only about seven kilometres east, which makes this the easy first stop of a circuit that gets wilder with every mile.

There is a legend attached to the bay that every local will be happy to tell you. In the old stories of the Fianna, the great Daire Donn landed a huge invading force at Ventry, and the Fianna defended the strand for a year and a day in what is remembered as the Battle of Ventry. Whether or not you believe in a year-long battle, the place feels like it was made for such a story, flat and open and watched from above by the hills.

On the bike the road is the R559, and the character is typical west Kerry: narrow, walled, and busy enough in July that you will spend part of the day tucked in behind a hire car or a tour bus. Most traffic runs the loop anticlockwise to keep the coaches from meeting each other on the tight sections, so riding clockwise is likely to put you face to face with them. Early morning, before ten, is when the whole thing feels like a proper road rather than a queue. The bends are gentle and the surface is generally fine, with the odd bump where the Atlantic weather has been at it.

Ventry is part of the Gaeltacht, the Irish-speaking region, and you will hear the language in shops and on the road signs, which are often only in Irish. Greet people and you will be rewarded. Dingle has the fuel, the shops and the harbour restaurants, so top up there before heading round, because the stretch beyond Ventry has very little. A cafe or two near the beach does the job for coffee, and in summer there are usually food vans.

If the light is clear you can see the Blasket Islands ahead as you leave, grey shapes on the water that you will soon be much closer to.
t.slea head@52.1,-10.5:
Slea Head is the western end of Europe in everything but the strict geographical sense, and on a clear day it feels like it. The road clings to the side of Mount Eagle high above the Atlantic, and to the south-west the Blasket Islands lie spread across the water, with Skellig Michael faint on the horizon when the air is very clean. The Irish name is Ceann Sléibhe, the head of the mountain, and the headland drops into the sea in a tumble of rock, bracken and stone-walled fields that look too small to farm.

There is a small cross and a shrine at the viewpoint, and a car park that is always more crowded than you would like. Pull in anyway, because this is the best view on the whole peninsula. The islands on the water are the Blaskets, once home to a community of Irish speakers who produced some of the most remarkable literature in the language. The film Ryan's Daughter was shot along this stretch in the late 1960s, which is part of the reason the beaches below the road, at Coumeenoole, look familiar even if you have never been.

It is not a place to hurry. Meeting a coach in the wrong spot is routine, and the ride rewards patience and an easy rhythm far more than pace. Gusts off the ocean can be strong on the headland, and sea mist sometimes rolls up the slope and wipes the view out in minutes. A morning with a light westerly and sun is about as good as riding gets.

t.dunquin@52.1,-10.5:
Dunquin, in Irish Dún Chaoin, is the last village before the road turns north, and it has the look of a place that has been hanging on at the edge of things for a very long time. The houses are scattered down a hillside above a cove, and the pier below is reached by a steep, zigzagging track that has been a postcard staple for decades. From here the boats once crossed to the Blasket Islands, a mile or two offshore across a stretch of water that can be calm one hour and furious the next.

The islanders left behind a literary legacy out of all proportion to their number, with books like An tOileánach, by Tomás Ó Criomhthain, and Peig by Peig Sayers, which every Irish schoolchild has met, willingly or not. The Blasket Centre in Dunquin tells the story well and is worth an hour if the weather turns. It sits right on the road, with a cafe, and the view from its windows is hard to beat.

The road drops and climbs through small bends, with views across the sound that change on every corner, and the surface is mostly good. Parking at the pier is tight, so leave the bike at the top and walk down if you want a look. Sheep and tourists are the two main hazards. In summer the village is lively; out of season it can be nearly silent, and the weather can strip the colour from the landscape in an afternoon.

Fuel is not available in the village, and the nearest dependable pumps are in Dingle, about thirteen kilometres away. If you need a sit-down meal or a bed, Dunquin has a small youth hostel and a handful of guesthouses, and the cafe at the Blasket Centre is a good fallback.

There is something faintly humbling about standing here. Few places have so little between you and the other side of the Atlantic, and the cliffs and the sea still do exactly what they did when the islanders rowed out in their naomhóga, the tarred canvas boats built for these waters.
t.ballyferriter@52.2,-10.4:
Past Dunquin the road leaves the high cliffs and swings north into gentler country, and Ballyferriter, Baile an Fheirtéaraigh, is the first real village on that side. Peninsula life is slow here, and a coffee stop tends to turn into a longer chat than you meant.

The riding is easy and pleasant. The road is narrow and enclosed by hedgerows rather than walls, with broad open bends and little traffic away from the busy coastal strip, so you can relax a bit after the exposure of Slea Head. The light is best in the late afternoon, when the low sun picks out the stone walls and lights the Three Sisters hills across the bay.
