t.tad fane@15.2,106.1:
Two rivers run off the Bolaven Plateau side by side and throw themselves into the same gorge, and the result is Tad Fane, one of the tallest waterfalls in Laos, with a drop of well over a hundred metres. The streams, called the Huay Champi and the Huay Bang Lieng, plunge in thin white ribbons from the rim into a deep green abyss, and from a lookout across the gorge you can watch them fall for what seems like a very long time. The sound arrives a moment late, the spray drifts up on the air, and the mist lingers in the trees at the bottom. The best view is in the rainy season, from about June to October, when the flow is at its fullest, though the dry season gives clearer skies.

The plateau is a world apart from the flat, hot lowlands of southern Laos. At around a thousand metres or more, the air is cooler and the red volcanic soil is perfect for coffee, tea, cardamom and bananas, and the road from Pakse climbs through plantations and forest to reach it. It is called Bolaven, which means the place of the Laven people, one of the ethnic groups that live here, along with the Alak, Katu and others, each with their own villages, languages and customs. The French introduced coffee in the early twentieth century, and it is still the main crop.

The riding on the plateau is a pleasure. The main roads are paved and quiet, winding through forest and coffee farms, and the side tracks are dirt, often red and slippery after rain. Distances are modest, and the cool air is a relief after the heat of Pakse. In the wet season, storms come in the afternoon and the roads can be muddy, so start early. Watch for water buffalo, children, dogs and the occasional pig. Laos is also the most heavily bombed country in the world per capita, because of the American campaigns of the 1960s and 70s, and unexploded ordnance is still a danger in some rural areas, so stay on established paths and roads.

There is a resort and a small restaurant near the viewing point, and basic food stalls appear along the road. Fuel is available in Pakxong, about eleven kilometres away, which has stations, shops and cafes, and also in Pakse, thirty-six kilometres to the west, where a wider choice is on offer. Carry cash in Lao kip, since cards are rarely accepted.

Evening on the plateau is cool, and a hot cup of local coffee is the right way to end the day.
t.paksong@15.2,106.2:
Paksong, which is also spelled Pakxong, is the unofficial coffee capital of Laos, a dusty market town set at the heart of the Bolaven Plateau where the air is cool, the soil is red and the whole economy smells of roasting beans. The plateau rises to over a thousand metres and catches regular rain, which suits both Arabica and Robusta, and the French planters who began growing coffee here in the early twentieth century left a legacy that Lao farmers have turned into a thriving industry. Plantations of shiny dark green bushes cover the hillsides, and in the harvest season, red berries are spread on tarpaulins to dry beside the road.

The town itself is simple, with a main street of shops and cafes, a busy market, and the sort of ordinary friendliness that comes with having few tourists. It makes a good base for the plateau, with guesthouses, noodle stalls and places to buy fresh coffee beans to take home. A cup of strong local coffee, often served with sweet condensed milk, is a morning ritual. Tea is grown here too, as is cardamom, and fruit and vegetables from the cool slopes are sold at the market, including strawberries and cabbage that would not survive in the lowlands.

The ride to Paksong from Pakse is a good one, climbing for about fifty kilometres from the Mekong plain onto the plateau, through villages and forest, with the temperature dropping noticeably. The road is generally paved and decent, though there are patches of damage and the occasional pothole, and trucks carrying coffee and produce share the route with motorbikes and minibuses. In the rainy season, from May to October, the downpours can be heavy and landslides are possible on the slopes. The dry season, from November to April, is the best time, with clearer skies and easier roads.

Paksong has fuel stations, shops, banks and basic guesthouses, which makes it the main service point on the plateau. The next sizeable place on the loop, Ban Thateng, is a small town with fewer facilities, so fill here and carry some cash. Phone coverage is reasonable in the town but may fade in the countryside.

If you have time, visit one of the coffee farms on the outskirts, where growers will show you the process from berry to cup. The farmers are proud of their product, and a tour is a good way to understand what the plateau is about.
t.tad lo@15.5,106.3:
Tad Lo is a place where the Bolaven Plateau puts on its gentlest face. The Xe Set river tumbles over a series of low waterfalls and rapids in a wooded setting, with simple guesthouses on the banks, a few small restaurants and a village atmosphere that is popular with travellers who want to slow down. The falls are not the largest in Laos, but they are among the most pleasant, since you can swim in the pools below them in the dry season, sit on the rocks with a cold drink and listen to the water. The name tad means waterfall in Lao, and the plural is well deserved, since there are a handful in the neighbourhood.

The people here are mostly of the Katu and Alak ethnic groups, who live in villages nearby and keep their own customs, including a tradition of keeping elephants, which have long been used for work in the forest. A few operators run elephant-related activities, and travellers should think carefully about which ones treat the animals well. The villages can be visited, but it is polite to go with a local guide and to ask before taking photographs of people.

The riding is a pleasant part of the Bolaven loop. The roads around Tad Lo are paved, narrow and quiet, with rolling hills, forest and farmland, and side tracks are dirt and sometimes steep. The surface can be rough in places, particularly after the rains, and the red clay becomes slippery when wet. Motorbikes are the ordinary transport here, and you will share the road with local riders carrying astonishing loads. Cattle, buffalo and chickens use the road freely, so keep your speed modest and expect surprises. The best time is the dry season, from November to April, when the roads are firm and the skies are clear. The rainy season brings green hills and full falls but also mud and leeches.

For practical needs, Tad Lo has guesthouses with simple rooms, restaurants serving noodle soup, fried rice and grilled fish, and a few shops. Fuel is not reliably available in the village, and the nearest stations are in Ban Thateng and in Salavan, about twenty-six kilometres away, a small provincial town with markets and basic services. It is wise to fill before you head out and to carry a little extra if you plan to explore the side roads.

Evenings are quiet, with the sound of the river and the occasional cry of a gibbon from the forest. It is a good place to break the loop and linger.
t.waterville coast@51.8,-10.2:
The coast near Waterville is where the Ring of Kerry earns its reputation. The road runs along a narrow strip between the mountains and the sea, and on a clear day the views open across Ballinskelligs Bay toward the Skellig Islands, two jagged rocks that rise from the Atlantic about twelve kilometres offshore. The larger of them, Skellig Michael, holds the remains of an early medieval monastery, perched among the cliffs, where monks lived in stone beehive huts above the roaring sea. It is one of the most remarkable monastic sites anywhere, and it can be seen from the road on a good day.

Waterville is a small seaside town, with a long promenade, a few cafes, and a statue of Charlie Chaplin, who holidayed here with his family in the 1960s and fell in love with the place. Lough Currane, a large freshwater lake behind the town, is famous for its salmon and sea trout, and the surrounding hills are dotted with ancient ring forts and stone crosses. The people here speak both Irish and English, and the culture of music, storytelling, and tea with brown bread is still strong.

The riding is superb but needs attention. The road from Waterville toward Cahersiveen climbs and dips along the coast, with long bends, steep descents, and sometimes a surface that is patched or bumpy. Near Coomakista Pass, the view opens over the sea and islands, and there is a lay-by that is worth a stop. The weather can change in minutes: sunshine can give way to driving rain, and the wind off the Atlantic can be strong. Coach traffic in summer slows everything, so early starts help.

Fuel is available in Waterville and Cahersiveen, about fourteen kilometres away, and it is wise to fill up before riding the more remote parts of the coast. Dingle, across the water to the north, is the next larger place, though it is a long way round by road. There are plenty of cafes and pubs for lunch, and a bowl of seafood chowder is a good bet. Late spring and early autumn offer the best light and the fewest crowds. Wear good waterproofs, and let the weather decide the pace.
t.kerry cliffs@51.8,-10.3:
The Kerry Cliffs are the sort of place that makes you stop talking. They rise about three hundred metres from the Atlantic, near the western tip of the Iveragh Peninsula, a wall of old red sandstone that drops almost vertically into the sea. Out beyond the edge, the Skellig rocks stand like two stone sails, Skellig Michael with its early monastery clinging to the summit, and its smaller companion crowded with seabirds. The Kerry Cliffs are a good place to see them without the crowds, with gannets, fulmars and choughs wheeling below.

A short walk from the car park leads along a path to a series of viewing platforms, and the wind here is a permanent part of the scenery. The path is on private land, and there is a small entrance fee, which I would not argue with. Keep back from the edge, because gusts can be fierce, the ground is soft after rain, and there are no safety walls.

Getting here is half the pleasure. Most tourists follow the famous Ring of Kerry in the same direction, with convoys of coaches in summer. The Skellig Ring is a quieter loop off the main road, through Portmagee and Ballinskelligs, with small, narrow and rolling roads along the coast, wide Atlantic views and often not another vehicle for miles. The surface is variable, with patched tarmac, a few tight bends and sheep on the road, so ride at a pace that lets you look. The wind and weather are changeable. A sunny morning can turn to driving rain in twenty minutes, and the light between showers is some of the best in Ireland. Midweek in May, June or September is best.

Portmagee is a small harbour village with pubs serving seafood and good coffee, and it is the departure point for boat trips to the Skelligs, weather permitting. Cahersiveen, about sixteen kilometres away, is the nearest town with proper fuel and supplies, and I would not rely on pumps closer to the cliffs. Fill up before you come out here.

The landscape around is old, bare and green, and the weather arrives from America across the open sea. It is worth sitting still for a few minutes and watching the water change colour.
t.bassari country bassari@12.6,-12.8:
Where south-eastern Senegal meets Guinea, the flat savannah gives way to the first hills of the Fouta Djallon, and in these hills live the Bassari, a people who have kept their own beliefs, language and rituals despite centuries of pressure from surrounding powers. The Bassari Country, together with the lands of the Bedik and Fula peoples, is a World Heritage cultural landscape on the Senegalese side, and the same hill country carries on across the border; the coordinates place you in Guinea, in the remote country west of Youkounkoun. Villages of round huts with conical thatched roofs sit on hillsides among terraced fields of fonio, millet and peanuts, and the year is punctuated by initiation ceremonies in which masked figures in costumes of leaves and fibres come out of the sacred forest.

The landscape is wild and beautiful. In the rainy season, roughly June to October, everything turns green, rivers swell and waterfalls such as Dindéfello, just over the border in Senegal, pour down cliffs. In the dry season the grass turns gold, fires sweep through the bush, and the air fills with dust and haze. To the north lies Niokolo-Koba National Park, one of the largest protected areas in West Africa, home to antelopes, hippos, chimpanzees and, in small numbers, lions and elephants.

This is serious adventure riding. Roads in the area are mostly laterite tracks, red dirt that turns to slippery mud in the rainy season and corrugated, dusty washboard in the dry season. River crossings can be impassable after heavy rain. Border crossings between Senegal and Guinea are possible but slow, with paperwork and checkpoints, and it is wise to travel with local knowledge and plenty of patience. Breakdowns are your own problem, so carry tools, spare tubes and enough water for long days.

Fuel is scarce. Fill up in the larger towns, such as Kédougou in Senegal or Koundara and Youkounkoun in Guinea, and carry extra; in villages, petrol is often sold in bottles or jerry cans by the roadside, of uncertain quality. Food is simple: rice with peanut sauce, fonio, grilled meat and fresh fruit in season. Greet people properly, ask permission before taking pictures, especially of ceremonies, and remember that you are a guest in a place where tradition still matters deeply.
t.peul dindefello@12.4,-12.3:
Dindéfello is where the Sahel finally gives up and the Fouta Djallon begins. The village sits in southeastern Senegal, tucked against the border with Guinea, and the plateau behind it drops away in a red cliff that feeds a waterfall of about a hundred metres. After the rains the fall is a proper white rope hanging off the rock. In the dry season it thins to a veil, but the pool beneath is still deep enough for a cool plunge and the walk through the gorge in the shade is worth the heat.

The village itself is Peul, the Fulani herders and farmers who run cattle across this whole belt of West Africa, and you will meet them in the lanes with long staves and slow greetings. Behind them live chimpanzees, a small community of the savannah type that has adapted to open woodland, and the local community runs a reserve and guiding programme around them. You are very unlikely to see them from a motorcycle, and nobody should promise otherwise. What you will see are baboons on the rocks, hornbills, and a lot of light, the late-afternoon kind that turns the laterite orange.

Getting here is the real trip. The closest proper town is Kédougou, about twenty-seven kilometres away, with a market, fuel and a handful of places to eat and sleep. From there the road runs south and up onto the escarpment, with a mix of tarmac and stretches of red dirt, depending on the season and recent grading. In the rains the surface can turn greasy and rutted, and river crossings can be a problem. In the dry months it is dusty, corrugated, and lovely. Carry water, carry spare fuel from Kédougou because the village will not have a pump, and allow double the time that the map suggests.

Dindéfello makes a good base for a day on foot, with the waterfall in the morning and the plateau edge for sunset. The Bassari and the Niokolo-Koba park lie in the same corner of the country, so this stop works as both an ending and a beginning. Ask locally before you swim, keep to the guide on the cliff paths, and leave early enough to be back on a good road before dark, since cattle and goats sleep on the warm tarmac at night.
t.complex of hue monuments@16.5,107.6:
The Perfume River bends around the old capital of Vietnam like a hand around a cup, and the Citadel of Hué sits on its north bank behind moats and thick brick walls. This is the heart of the Complex of Hué Monuments, the seat of the Nguyen emperors, who ruled from here from the early nineteenth century until the last of them abdicated in 1945. Inside the walls is the Imperial City, and inside that the Forbidden Purple City, where only the court was allowed. The Ngo Mon gate, with its upper pavilion where proclamations were made, is the grand entrance, and it is worth walking through on foot rather than just photographing from the saddle.

Much of the interior was lost in the fighting of the Tet Offensive in 1968, when the citadel was held for weeks and badly damaged. You see it in the gaps: lawns where halls once stood, walls still pocked, restoration going on in patches. That unevenness is part of the charm, and it makes the intact buildings feel like survivors. The complex was listed by UNESCO in 1993, and tickets are sold at the gate.

Riding here is a city ride, and a good one if you are calm about it. Hué is a place of 287,000 people and, it sometimes seems, as many scooters, and the streets around the citadel are flat, wide and busy. Traffic flows in a loose, negotiated way. Move at the speed of the people around you, keep a steady line and do not make sudden decisions, and it works. Fuel is easy in town, with stations on every main road, and parking next to the gate is usually sorted out by whoever is waiting there.

Come early or late. Midday heat in the central Vietnamese lowlands is heavy, and the light on the brickwork is best an hour after sunrise or in the late afternoon. Afterwards, find a bowl of bun bo Hue, the spicy beef and lemongrass noodle soup this city is proud of, and sit for a while. The riverside is only a few minutes away, and a slow evening crossing of the bridges is the right way to finish.
t.gia long tomb@16.4,107.6:
Emperor Gia Long, who founded the Nguyen dynasty and reunified Vietnam in 1802, chose a spot for his tomb about eleven kilometres from Hué, and he chose it far from the city on purpose. The Thien Tho hills rise south-west of the capital, and his burial ground lies tucked among them, a long, quiet complex of terraces, stone courtyards and guarding statues of mandarins and elephants. He died in 1820. His queen is buried beside him, which was unusual enough that guides still mention it.

Compared with the more elaborate tombs of his successors, Gia Long's is plain and weathered, and that is exactly why it appeals. Pine trees stand around the stone, moss is on the steps, and when you arrive there may be nobody else there at all. Much of the timber architecture has been lost over the years, and what remains is mostly stone and open ground. Take your time and look at the way the whole site was laid out to face the hills, with a lake in front, following the geomancy rules the court took seriously.

The ride out from Hué follows the river upstream, and this is where the day gets pleasant. You leave the flat grid of town behind and pass villages with gardens, small temples, fishing nets, and long stretches of road running under trees. It is not twisty in a mountain sense, but the surface is mostly decent, the traffic thins quickly, and you can enjoy the smell of woodsmoke and wet earth. Pay attention to water buffalo and children on bicycles in the villages, and to the occasional pothole after rain.

Fuel is in Hué, and I would fill up before leaving because there is nothing at the tomb. Bring water. You may find a drink seller near the entrance, though I would not count on it. Go in the morning, when the air is cooler and the hills are blue behind the stone, and give it an hour rather than ten minutes.
t.inuvik@68.4,-133.7:
Inuvik is the end of the road, quite literally. The Dempster Highway, a gravel road that runs for about 740 kilometres from near Dawson City through some of the wildest country in North America, finishes here, in the Mackenzie River delta, at the edge of the Arctic. The town was built in the 1950s to replace Aklavik, which was prone to flooding, and it was planned from scratch as an administrative centre, with a distinctive layout and utilidors, insulated pipes above ground that carry water and sewage, because the permafrost makes burying them impossible.

The population, about three thousand, is a mix of Gwich'in, Inuvialuit and settlers from the south. The best known building is the Igloo Church, officially Our Lady of Victory, finished in 1960, a white dome shaped like an igloo that is open to visitors. In summer, the sun does not set for several weeks, and in December, it does not rise. The Great Northern Arts Festival, held in July, brings artists from across the north.

Since 2017, a road has continued north from Inuvik to Tuktoyaktuk, on the Arctic Ocean, and it allows you to ride to the coast, touch the water and turn around. The Dempster itself is a serious proposition. The gravel surface can be loose, rutted or slick, tyres are damaged by sharp shale, and the weather can turn quickly. There are ferries across the Peel and Mackenzie rivers in summer, and ice roads in winter. Services are sparse, with fuel at Eagle Plains and Fort McPherson, so fill up at every opportunity and carry spare tyres, tubes and tools.

Inuvik itself has fuel, shops, a few places to eat and places to stay, though in summer, it is wise to book ahead. Mosquitoes are fierce in July. The best time to ride is from late June to August, when the road is clear and the days are long. Take warm layers, because it can be cold even in midsummer.
t.sceilg mhichil@51.8,-10.5:
Sceilg Mhichíl, in English Skellig Michael, is a pinnacle of rock rising out of the Atlantic about twelve kilometres off the Kerry coast, and it is one of those places that makes you wonder what kind of person would choose to live there. Monks did, starting somewhere around the sixth to eighth century, building a monastery of beehive-shaped stone huts, terraces and oratories on a ledge some two hundred metres above the waves, reached by roughly six hundred stone steps. They grew what they could, caught fish and birds, collected rainwater, and held services in some of the wildest conditions in Europe, until the community moved away in the thirteenth century. UNESCO listed the island in 1996.

From the mainland, the island is not something you ride to but something you ride toward. The coastal roads of south-west Kerry, such as the Skellig Ring around Portmagee and the Ring of Kerry itself, give long views across the water, and on a clear day the twin humps of Skellig Michael and Little Skellig stand out against the sea. Roads are narrow, winding and often shared with sheep, cyclists and tour buses, so the best approach is to ride slowly, use the pull-ins and avoid the main route in peak summer, when coaches follow each other in convoy. Weather is fickle, and sea mist can come in suddenly, making the bends greasy and the views vanish.

Landings on the island are limited to a small number of licensed boats from Portmagee and other harbours, only in the summer season and only when the sea is calm enough, and many days they are cancelled. Numbers are controlled, so booking well ahead is essential, and the climb is steep, with no handrails in places. If you cannot land, boat trips that circle the island still give a good view.

The nature is part of the story. Little Skellig holds one of the largest gannet colonies in the world, and Skellig Michael itself has puffins in summer, as well as shearwaters and storm petrels. The island has also found a modern audience as a film location for Star Wars, which gave the place a new wave of visitors.

Cahersiveen is the nearest town with fuel and a supermarket, and Portmagee, a small fishing village, has a couple of pubs for chowder and a pint while you wait for the weather.
t.bassari salemata@12.6,-12.8:
The Bassari people live in the hills of southeastern Senegal and northern Guinea, in a country of rocky outcrops, savannah and deep, lush valleys that run down from the Fouta Djallon plateau. Salemata is one of their main centres, a small town in the Kedougou region of Senegal, and the Bassari, with their neighbours the Bedik and the Fula, make up the cultural landscape of Bassari Country, listed by UNESCO in 2012. The Bassari have kept their traditions with great determination. Young men go through initiation rites in the forest, lasting weeks and ending with masked dances and ceremonies in which the whole village takes part. Dancers wear costumes of leaves and fibres, and the Bedik have their own, different, masks.

The landscape is attractive and dramatic, with low mountains, orange earth, tall baobabs and the dry-season haze known as the harmattan. Villages stand in the hills, built of mud and thatch, sometimes perched on ridges for defence, as they were in earlier centuries when slave raiders came. The Fula people live on the high plateau and have their own culture, with dances, song, and cattle herding. Further along, at Dindefello, a waterfall tumbles into a gorge, and chimpanzees live in the forests nearby.

Honest advice is needed on access. Roads in this corner of Africa are rough, and many are dirt tracks, which can become impassable in the rainy season, from June to October. Border areas can be unpredictable, and travellers should check the security situation with foreign office guidance before going. The nearest large settlement in the list, Youkounkoun, is more than thirty kilometres away, and services between are minimal. A properly prepared adventure bike with good tyres, spare fuel, a tool kit, water and a support plan is the only sensible approach. Fuel is best taken in the bigger towns, and Kedougou, the regional capital, is the place to stock up.

Visitors should behave carefully. Ask permission before taking photographs, particularly at ceremonies, and respect local rules about sacred places, which may be off limits. It is courteous to greet the village chief and explain your purpose. The dry season, from November to April, is the best time, though the heat builds towards May.
t.pakse@15.1,105.8:
Pakse sits where the Xe Don river meets the Mekong in the far south of Laos, a lazy, low-rise town of fewer than a hundred thousand people that works as the gateway to the Bolaven Plateau. The Mekong here is wide and brown, with sandbanks in the dry season, and a long bridge opened in 2000 with Japanese help carries the road over to the far bank. Streets are quiet, shuttered shops sell motorbike spares and coffee, and the pace is slow in a way that grows on you.

The plateau is the reason riders come. It rises to about a thousand metres east of town on old volcanic soil, and the cooler air and rich earth make it the heart of Lao coffee, along with tea, cardamom and fruit. The loop of roads over the plateau passes waterfalls such as Tad Fane, whose twin streams drop a hundred metres or so into a gorge, and Tad Yuang, a broad, easy cascade near the road. Villages of the Laven, Alak and Katu peoples line the route, with stilted houses and coffee beans drying on mats by the roadside.

The riding is a joy but demands attention. Surfaces range from smooth to broken tarmac, with potholes, gravel and occasional red mud after rain, and water buffalo, dogs and children share the way. The rainy season from May to October brings heavy afternoon downpours that wash out side roads, so mornings are best. November to February is cooler and dry, with brilliant light. Remember that this plateau was heavily bombed during the Vietnam war era, and the countryside still has unexploded ordnance, so stay on well-used tracks.

Pakse has all the services you could want: fuel stations on the main roads, guesthouses, riverside restaurants and bakeries serving the French-influenced baguette. Fill up here before climbing the plateau, since fuel in smaller villages is sold from roadside bottles and may be poor quality. Try a Lao coffee, strong and sweet with condensed milk, and a bowl of noodle soup. Wat Phou, the old Khmer temple at Champasak, is a half-day outing.
t.phong nha@17.6,106.3:
Phong Nha lies in central Vietnam in a country made of limestone, a landscape of jagged green peaks, hidden valleys and rivers that vanish underground. The village sits on the Son River, in Quang Binh province, and the nearest big town is Dong Hoi, about forty kilometres to the east on the coast. Behind it, the mountains rise toward the Laotian border, and the whole region was declared a World Heritage Site in 2003 for its caves and karst.

The caves are the reason people come, and there are genuinely extraordinary ones. Son Doong, found in 1991 by a local man and first explored by British cavers in 2009, is thought to be the largest cave passage in the world, big enough to hold a jungle and a skyscraper. Visiting it takes a permit, a guide and several days. Easier to see are Phong Nha Cave, reached by a long boat ride along the river, and Paradise Cave, with its long walkway through huge chambers of stalactites. Nearby, the Bong Lai valley has rice fields and buffalo, with a beautiful, slow feel.

The war left its mark. This area was on the Ho Chi Minh Trail, the supply network that ran through the mountains from north to south during the Vietnam War, and heavy American bombing hit the region. Craters still pock the fields and caves were used as hospitals and storage. Locals sheltered in the caves during the bombing, and old unexploded ordnance is still a hazard away from marked paths, so stay on established trails.

For riders, the Ho Chi Minh Road runs south from here through the mountains of the Central Highlands. It is a modern road built over the old trail, with long, smooth curves, forested slopes and little traffic compared with the coastal highway. Surface quality varies, with landslide patches, potholes and the occasional water buffalo or herd of cattle in the lane, so watch the road ahead. Mist hangs in the valleys in the early morning, and the light is often soft and hazy.

The rainy season, roughly from September to December, brings typhoons and flooding that can cut roads, while the dry season from March to August is hot, with strong sun. Fuel stations are in Dong Hoi and on the main road, but fill up whenever you see one on the mountain sections. Local food is simple and good, with rice noodle soups, grilled pork and the fresh river fish served at small family restaurants.
t.khai dinh tomb@16.4,107.6:
Khai Dinh's tomb is the last great monument of the Nguyen dynasty, and it is an odd, brilliant mixture of east and west. The emperor, who reigned from 1916 until 1925 under French protection, began building it in 1920 and it took more than a decade to finish, completed by his son Bao Dai. It sits on the slope of Chau Chu mountain, a few kilometers south of Hue, and is reached by a steep flight of stone stairs guarded by dragon balustrades and rows of stone mandarins, soldiers and horses.

Inside, the tomb breaks with tradition. It is built mostly of reinforced concrete, a modern material at the time, rather than the stone and brick of earlier tombs, and the interior is covered with a dazzling mosaic of broken porcelain and colored glass. Dragons coil across the ceiling, and paintings of nine dragons float above a gilded bronze statue of the emperor. The style mixes Vietnamese, Chinese, Indian and European elements, including Gothic columns and Roman arches. Critics at the time found it excessive, and the emperor was unpopular for taxing the people to build it, but today it is one of the most photographed sights in central Vietnam.

The ride from Hue is a pleasant one. The tombs lie along the Perfume River in a countryside of pine, rice fields and low hills, reached by narrow lanes that feel a long way from the city. In the morning the light is soft and the traffic light, though the road can be busy with tour buses by midday. The wet season runs from September to December, when typhoon rain and flooding are common, and the best months for riding are from February to May.

Hue, only about seven kilometers away, has fuel stations, cafes and a good range of food, including bun bo Hue, a spicy beef noodle soup that is a local pride. The climb to the tomb takes a short time and the heat can be considerable, so bring water. A small entrance fee applies.

When you reach the top, turn around. The view over the valley and the roofs of the pagodas is a quiet reward.
t.minh mang tomb@16.4,107.6:
If Khai Dinh's tomb is a showpiece, the tomb of Minh Mang is a work of calm. The second emperor of the Nguyen dynasty, who reigned from 1820 to 1841, planned it himself and died before it was finished, so his son completed it in the early 1840s. It sits on the bank of the Perfume River, about nine kilometers from Hue, in a landscape of lakes, pine and lawns that feels more like a park than a burial ground. Minh Mang was a stern ruler, a Confucian scholar who tried to centralize his state and promote traditional values, and his tomb reflects the order he valued.

The layout is strictly symmetrical, with a central axis running from the entrance gate through a series of courtyards, pavilions and bridges to the burial mound at the rear, which is enclosed in a circular wall and closed to visitors. Along the axis are stone steles, honor courts with statues of mandarins and elephants, and lakes crossed by covered bridges. The architecture borrows ideas from Chinese models but adapts them to the Vietnamese landscape, with water and trees as part of the design. The effect is a kind of ordered garden, quiet and green, and it is more moving than the grand scale suggests.

Getting there is part of the pleasure. The road from Hue runs beside the river through villages of conical-hatted farmers and small shrines, and the surface is mostly smooth with gentle curves. You can also reach the area by dragon boat from the city, though on a motorcycle the lanes are enjoyable in themselves. Go in the morning for cooler air and fewer tour groups. In the rainy season the lakes fill and the grass turns bright green, but typhoons can close roads and flood the lowlands.

The tomb is part of the Complex of Hue Monuments, which UNESCO listed in 1993. A small entrance fee applies, and the grounds are open most of the day. Fuel is easy to find in Hue, which has stations along its main roads and a lively food scene along the river.

The ride from here to Da Nang over the Hai Van Pass is one of the great coastal roads in Vietnam, with long curves above the sea and views of the bay, and it is a fine way to end the day.
t.hai van pass@16.2,108.1:
Hai Van means sea cloud, and from the summit the name makes perfect sense: the pass is a saddle in the Truong Son range where the mountains tumble straight into the South China Sea, and the clouds gather on the ridge like steam from a kettle. At around five hundred metres, it is not high, but it marks a real boundary. To the north, the weather tends to be cool and damp, with grey drizzle in winter, and to the south, around Da Nang, it is warmer and brighter. Locals say the pass splits the country's climate in two, and for much of the year they are right.

The road is the great motorcycle ride of central Vietnam, and it is a joy. From the Da Nang side, the old highway climbs in long, gentle bends through forest and scrub, with the bay and the peninsula of Son Tra spread below. Near the top, a café, souvenir stalls and an old stone gate and the remains of bunkers sit beside the road, with sweeping views to Lang Co in the north. The tarmac is good, the corners are medium and relaxed, and the road is wide enough for easy riding. Since the long tunnel opened in the mid-2000s, most trucks and buses use it, so the pass itself is quiet, mostly motorbikes and tour vans. Fog and rain can come in without warning, making the road slick, and early morning is the best time for clear views.

The pass has long been strategic. It was a frontier between the Viet and the Cham kingdoms, and a stone gate on the summit dates back centuries. The French built fortifications to control it, and during the Vietnam War its bunkers and watchtowers saw fighting. The old road was a lifeline for generations of travellers, and it became known to the wider world when the British television programme Top Gear filmed here in 2008 and called it one of the best coast roads in the world, which sent a wave of riders to try it for themselves.

Nature is lush and warm. The slopes are covered in tropical forest, and the sea below shifts between turquoise and slate depending on the light. The air smells of salt, wet leaves and frangipani, and on clear days you can see the long curve of the beach at Lang Co.

Buy fuel in Da Nang or Lang Co, since the pass has none. Wear a light rain jacket, bring water, and take it slowly; the road is shared with scooters, and the views are a big distraction.
t.lang co@16.2,108.1:
Lang Co is a long, thin sandbar of a village, with a lagoon on one side, the sea on the other, and the green wall of the Truong Son mountains rising behind both. It sits at the northern foot of the Hai Van Pass, on the road between Hue and Da Nang, and it has the relaxed, slightly sleepy air of a place that most travellers pass through on the way to somewhere else. That is a mistake, because the beach here is one of the loveliest in Vietnam, a wide curve of pale sand edged with casuarina trees, and the water is clear and warm for much of the year.

For riders it is a natural stop before or after the pass. The coastal highway arrives from the north, running along the lagoon on a narrow causeway with fishing boats and oyster beds on both sides, and the road is flat, straight and easy. The village has fuel, small restaurants, cafes and simple guesthouses, and it is a fine place for lunch before the climb. Traffic is a mix of scooters, trucks and tourist buses, so keep your attention up. The best time for a visit is spring and early summer, when the weather is warm and dry, while the autumn and winter months bring rain, wind and sometimes typhoons.

Lang Co is a fishing community, and its history is tied to the water. Families have long fished the lagoon and the sea, and oysters, crab and shrimp are the local specialities, often served grilled with chilli and lime on plastic stools by the roadside. The seafood here is fresh and cheap, and a plate of steamed crab with a cold drink is hard to beat. The old route from Hue crossed the sandbar on a track long before the modern road.

The lagoon is a shallow, calm stretch of brackish water, home to herons, egrets and other waders, and the mountains behind are covered in forest that catches the clouds. The air smells of salt, smoke from cooking fires and drying fish, and the sunsets across the water are glorious. In the evening, the light lingers, and fishing boats head out with lanterns.

Fill the tank here before the climb, bring a light jacket for the pass and give yourself time to walk on the beach. The pace is slow, and that is the point.
t.nakai@17.7,105.2:
Nakai is a name that belongs to a plateau, a reservoir and a small town all at once. It lies in Khammouane province, in central Laos, where the Annamite mountains rise toward the Vietnamese border, and the high, forested country around it is among the wildest in Southeast Asia. In 2010, the Nam Theun 2 dam closed its gates, flooding part of the Nakai plateau and creating a large reservoir whose margin is still dotted with the stumps of drowned trees. The surrounding protected area shelters rare animals, including some, such as the saola, so elusive that it was only described by science in the 1990s.

The Thakhek Loop, the popular motorbike route that circles this province, passes through here, and for riders it is a change of pace. The tarmac is generally good, with smooth bends and long stretches of open road through rice paddies, teak and bamboo, with limestone karst rising in fantastic shapes. Heat and humidity are constants, with the dry season from November to February the most comfortable, and the wet season bringing sudden downpours and mud. Watch out for water buffalo, children, chickens, dogs and the occasional slow truck.

Villages are made of wooden houses on stilts, with big tin roofs, and many families are from ethnic minorities with their own languages and customs. Sticky rice, grilled meat and spicy dipping sauces are the staples of the roadside food stalls, and strong Lao coffee, often sweetened with condensed milk, is the best stimulant. In the evening, smoke from cooking fires drifts across the fields, and the sound of frogs and insects takes over from the engines.

Nakai is a town big enough to offer the basics: fuel stations, small shops, noodle stalls and a few simple guesthouses. Since the stretches between towns can be long, it is wise to fill up here, and to carry a small spare supply if your bike has a limited range. Cash in kip is more useful than cards. Rest in the shade in the afternoon heat, drink more than you think you need, and aim to finish the day's ride before dusk, since unlit roads and animals make night riding unwise.
t.thalang@18.0,105.0:
Thalang is a crossing point on the Thakhek Loop, a place where a few houses, a handful of shops and a patch of rice field mark the spot where the road swings toward the great limestone country. It lies in Khammouane province, in central Laos, in the zone where the Hinboun river and its reservoir cut through towering karst, and the fields in front of the cliffs are green in the wet season and golden after harvest. The label may be modest, but the setting is anything but.

The geology is the story. The Phou Hin Poun protected area, a vast plateau of limestone that has been dissolved by rain into spires, caves, sinkholes and underground rivers, covers much of the region, and the road passes beside it, with wall after wall of grey rock draped in forest. Mist often clings to the tops in the morning. It is a landscape of the kind you find in northern Vietnam, but with far fewer people and a gentler pace. Caves with streams, swimming holes and viewpoints appear along the way if you are willing to follow a side track.

The riding is easy and delightful. The road wanders through villages and fields with long, flowing bends, a smooth surface for the most part, and a constant rotation of buffalo, bicycles and women carrying baskets. In the heat of the day, the air is thick, and the shade of a roadside shelter is welcome. The cooler dry season, from November to February, is the best time, while the rainy months can bring flash floods, mud and leeches on the trails.

As for services, Thalang is a small place, so do not rely on a full range. Fuel is sometimes sold from drums or bottles at roadside shops, which is a practical, if unscientific, arrangement, and it is best to arrive with a good tank. Food stalls serve noodle soup, grilled chicken and sticky rice, and you can usually buy cold drinks and water. Simple guesthouses are nearby. Make time to stop, take off your helmet and listen: in the quiet of the afternoon you will hear roosters, cicadas and the faint thrum of a distant motorbike.
t.hai van pass point 3@16.2,108.1:
Lang Co is a thin spit of sand between the South China Sea and a wide, still lagoon, tucked on the northern side of the Hai Van mountains, and for many riders it is the reward at the bottom of the pass. The beach runs for miles, pale and almost empty outside the summer weekends, and behind it the lagoon is dotted with fish farms, oyster stakes and stilt houses. Behind, the green mountains rise steeply, usually with a cloud lying on the ridge. The village is small, but there is fuel, and a line of seafood restaurants along the road serves crab, clams and grilled fish.

The descent from the pass to the lagoon is one of the best parts of the ride. The road drops through hairpins and long sweeps with the sea in view, and once down it becomes flat and open, running beside the beach and the railway line. The Vietnamese north-south railway, the Reunification Express, clings to the coast here, and the sight of a train curving along the shore is a famous photograph. Keep an eye on the surface after rain, since leaves and mud can lie on the bends.

The tunnel under the pass, opened in 2005 and about six kilometres long, comes out near Lang Co, and its mouth is visible from the lagoon. The area has long been a fishing community, and in the old days it was a stop on the imperial road between Hue and Da Nang. Many travellers spend a night here, enjoying the quiet.

Food is simple and excellent. Try a plate of steamed clams with lemongrass, or a bowl of the local noodles, then a coffee on a hammock by the beach. Afternoon storms roll in from the sea in autumn, so check the sky. In summer, the beach is hot and the sea warm, and in winter, the north wind brings grey skies and cool days. Spring is the most pleasant season.
t.thakhek loop point 2@17.7,105.2:
The Nakai plateau is a high, forested tableland in the middle of Laos, and the coordinates lie in its heart, close to the small town of Nakai. For years, this was a remote area of thinly populated forest and grassland, home to ethnic minority communities and wildlife. In the 2000s it was transformed by the Nam Theun 2 project, a large dam and hydroelectric scheme that flooded the central part of the plateau and created a reservoir of several hundred square kilometres, and the villagers were resettled. The water is calm and still, ringed by drowned trees and low green hills, with a bit of an eerie beauty.

The road across the plateau is straight and wide by Lao standards, with a surface that is mostly good and light traffic. Trucks carrying timber or building materials go past occasionally, but you can ride for long periods without seeing another vehicle. Corners are few, and the main challenge is dogs, chickens, water buffalo and sometimes children on the road. After rain, mud can cover the verges, and bridges can be narrow with missing planks. Heat and humidity are strong in the middle of the day, so drink water and wear light, ventilated gear.

Wildlife here is rich, because the plateau is surrounded by protected areas, including Nakai-Nam Theun National Biodiversity Conservation Area. The forests hold gibbons, elephants, tigers in tiny numbers, and one of the most famous recent finds in zoology, the saola, a rare forest bovine first described by scientists in the early 1990s in the mountains nearby. You will not see these animals from the road, but the quiet of the forest is a pleasure in itself.

Services are basic. The town has small shops, noodle stalls, and a fuel stop, though supplies may be limited, so fill up in Thakhek or at the bigger service points. Accommodation consists of simple guesthouses. In the dry season, from November to February, the air is clear and the roads in good condition. In the wet season, expect floods, leeches and mud.
t.thakhek loop point 3@18.0,105.0:
Ban Na Hin is the small market town where the Thakhek Loop turns toward its most famous attraction, and it sits on Route 13 at the foot of a limestone ridge. A cluster of guesthouses, noodle shops and fuel stalls line the highway, and riders stop to eat, refuel and chat with other travellers before the turn to Konglor. The town is quiet, with few buildings of any size, but it is surrounded by amazing scenery of sheer limestone cliffs rising from green fields and forests.

The limestone massif behind the town is the Phou Hin Bun national protected area, a vast, rugged karst landscape of towers, sinkholes and caves that stretches toward Vietnam. Many of the caves are still unexplored, and wildlife survives in the dense forest. The rock is old seabed, laid down hundreds of millions of years ago and thrust up as the Indian plate pushed into Asia, and then worn by rain into needles and domes. The scenery is especially fine in the early morning, when mist fills the valleys and the cliffs rise out of it.

The road along Route 13 is a main north-south highway, and here it is a fast, well-surfaced road with long, gentle curves, but with trucks and buses that run quickly. Take care at the junction with the Konglor road, where traffic enters from the side. Watch for animals and for motorbikes without lights at dusk. The roadside stalls sell sticky rice cooked in bamboo, grilled chicken, and papaya salad with chilli that can burn your lips.

Practical matters are straightforward. There is fuel here, and it is wise to fill up fully before heading for the cave, because the road beyond is long and remote. Simple guesthouses provide a bed and a fan. Evenings are warm, with a chorus of frogs and insects, and the night sky is clear. The hot season brings temperatures above thirty-five degrees, and the rainy season brings mud. The cool season is the best time.
t.bolaven plateau loop point 4@15.5,106.3:
Beyond Ban Thateng, the plateau tilts north and the landscape becomes quieter, with fewer tourists and more forest. The coordinates lie on a long, rolling stretch of road between Thateng and Salavan, where rubber and coffee plantations alternate with patches of dense forest and fields of rice and cassava. Villages here belong to the Katu, Alak and Ta-oy people, who speak Mon-Khmer languages and keep traditions that outsiders are only beginning to document. Many houses are built on stilts with thatched or tin roofs, and buffalo wander through the yards.

The road is a mix of good and bad. Some sections are smooth and new, while others are patched with holes that can swallow a wheel. Gravel gathers on bends, and heavy trucks hauling timber and produce churn up dust in the dry season. Visibility can be poor in the dry season haze, when farmers burn fields, and in the wet season low cloud fills the valleys. Wear a face cover for the dust, and carry water.

The nearest town of any size is Salavan, which has a market, simple guesthouses and fuel, and Thateng is a small village with limited services. Tad Lo, a pleasant cluster of waterfalls on the Xe Set river with guesthouses and a pleasant swimming spot, lies a little way to the south and is one of the most relaxed places on the loop. Elephants are sometimes used for rides there, though it is worth considering how these animals are treated.

The history of the area echoes through its landscape. The Ho Chi Minh Trail ran through the mountains to the east, and the hills carry the scars of wartime bombing, with craters now grown over by grass and trees. Today, life is simple and agricultural. Stop for a bowl of noodle soup or a fresh coconut when you find a stall, because they can be few and far between. Early mornings, with mist on the hills and the sound of roosters, are a lovely time to ride.
